Need to search first.I've written notes for every verse except v. 15, where I found nothing specific. Two limits shaped what's here:

- **Tool limit.** I hit the research tool's usage cap early. Most notes come from the excerpts the search returned, not full pages. I read only one page in full: the Enduring Word chapter page, and even that cut off partway through v. 20. A point not appearing here may simply mean I didn't see it.
- **No Catholic, Orthodox, netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org pages, and nothing on prosperity or hyper-grace teaching.** Leaving those out is not a sign the sources say nothing. The only "modern scholarship" here is a NET Bible note quoted on Precept Austin and the Expositor's Greek Testament.

The pages rarely state which tradition a writer belongs to. Clarke is the only one labelled (StudyLight calls him "Wesleyan/Methodist"). Otherwise I give the site's group from your list and don't add my own labels.

---

## Luke 6:1–24 — Research notes

**v. 1 (grainfields; "second-first Sabbath" in older texts)**
- **"Second Sabbath."** Guzik suggests it may count the Sabbaths since Luke 4:31, showing how busy Jesus had been. He adds that Clarke and others take it as the first Sabbath after Passover, and that because of textual problems it may simply mean "on the Sabbath." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Picking the grain.** Guzik says the picking itself wasn't wrong: Deuteronomy 23:25 allowed the poor to glean, so it wasn't stealing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Ellicott** says the phrase appears in no other writer, so its meaning is largely guesswork. The grain was ripe but not yet harvested, which puts the scene between Passover and Pentecost. He notes that some important manuscripts leave the word out, but argues that a hard reading is more likely to be original. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-1.htm
- **Gill** reports wide disagreement. He explains a counting system in which Sabbaths were numbered from the second day of the feast up to Pentecost, so this was the "second-first." Citing Jewish rules, he says rubbing and blowing away the chaff on the Sabbath was what drew the complaint. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html
- **Others on the same page.** Benson cites Epiphanius, who placed this on the Sabbath after the second day of Unleavened Bread. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown calls the phrase obscure but gives the usual explanation. Meyer's notes list Calvin among those who held a different view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-1.htm
- **Kelly's textual note** credits Meyer with the theory that a scribe accidentally wrote a word twice. Kelly adds that other scholars keep the common reading. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kelly/luke/6.htm

**v. 2 (the Pharisees' objection)**
- **Precept Austin** points out a difference from the other Gospels. In Matthew and Mark the charge is aimed at Jesus. In Luke the "you" is plural, covering Jesus and the disciples. It calls the rules being broken man-made. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Guzik** says the problem was the day, not the act. Under the rabbis' lists, one mouthful counted as four violations: reaping, threshing, winnowing and preparing food. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Pett** suggests the Pharisees may have been walking with the group, watching for faults. He adds that Jesus, as their teacher, was held responsible. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/luke-6.html
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes that the rule allegedly broken was not one God had given. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-6.html

**vv. 3–4 (David and the consecrated bread)**
- **Guzik** sees a rebuke of men proud of their Bible knowledge. His first principle is that human need matters more than religious ritual. He thinks the David story fits because it was about eating, probably happened on a Sabbath (1 Sam 21:6), and involved David's companions too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin** notes that David broke an actual law of Moses (Lev 24:5–9), while the disciples broke only a human rule. It also cites Stein: Luke adds "only" to stress David's breach, which makes the One greater than David look greater still. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Pulpit Commentary:** no ceremonial law should override the body's basic needs. It notes that Matthew adds "I desire mercy, not sacrifice." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/6.htm
- **Coffman** says the Pharisees excused David's real breach while accusing the innocent disciples. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-6.html
- **Kelly** says God would not hold to ritual while His anointed king went hungry. He calls Jesus the rejected Son of David, as free as the rejected David. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/kelly/luke/6.htm
- **Preacher's Homiletical** adds that 1 Samuel 21:6 suggests David's visit also fell on a Sabbath. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/luke-6.html

**v. 5 (Lord of the Sabbath)**
- **A claim to be God.** Guzik calls it a direct claim to deity. Coffman notes that "Lord" comes first in the Greek, for emphasis. He says Jesus explained the law's true meaning rather than setting it aside. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/ ; https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-6.html
- **Precept Austin** sees a messianic claim. Since Jesus is Creator (Col 1:16), He made the Sabbath and has the right to rule it. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** sees a claim to the authority of the Lawgiver at Sinai. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-5.htm
- **Constable** (quoting another writer): like David, Jesus could set Sabbath rules aside to fulfil a greater calling from God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-5.html
- **Expositor's Greek Testament** (older critical scholarship) observes that in Luke the saying is simply tacked on, where in Matthew it caps the argument. It suggests Luke left out Mark's "Sabbath was made for man" because Gentile readers might find it hard to follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-5.htm
- **Where Protestant writers differ: does the Sabbath still bind Christians?**
  - *It continues as the Lord's Day.* Matthew Henry says it is still Christ's day, renamed the Lord's Day and moved to the first day of the week, but still a rest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-5.html
  - *A Sabbath remains, reshaped.* Preacher's Homiletical says Christ recognised the Sabbath's obligation and did not abolish it. He changed it into a means of grace, and His followers moved it to the first day. It quotes W. Taylor: "there is still a Sabbath day for us." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/luke-6.html
  - *The old law is no longer binding.* A writer quoted on Precept Austin says that, because Christ is the true Sabbath rest, the old Sabbath law is no longer needed or binding. It was reinstituted as the Lord's Day, a day of worship. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
  - *Not a licence for anyone.* Pulpit Commentary's R.M. Edgar warns against reading "Son of Man" as letting any person treat the Sabbath as they please. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/luke-6.html

**v. 6 (the withered hand)**
- **Guzik** notes that Jesus kept going to synagogue despite the growing hostility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin** says healing the man backed up Jesus' claim to lordship just made. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 7 (watching to accuse)**
- **Precept Austin** says the Greek tense shows they watched Him continually. It quotes the NET Bible note: the Mishnah allowed healing on the Sabbath only when life was in danger. It quotes Bock with a similar list of exceptions. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Guzik:** by watching, they admitted He could heal. He cites Pate's suggestion that they may have planted the man there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Gill:** they hoped to accuse Him as they had accused the disciples. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html

**v. 8 (he knew their thoughts; "stand among us")**
- **Pett:** Jesus could have told the man to come back after sunset, but that would have granted that the rabbis were right. So He called him out in public. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/luke-6.html

**v. 9 (do good or evil?)**
- **Guzik:** there is never a wrong day to do real good. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Pett** links the question to imagery of withered and fruitful trees. https://studylight.org/commentaries/pet/luke-6.html
- **Coffman** quotes Miller: while Jesus was saving life on the Sabbath, His enemies were using it to plot His death. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-6.html
- **An unnamed writer on Precept Austin** draws the lesson that works of mercy are lawful on the Sabbath. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 10 ("Stretch out your hand")**
- **Guzik:** Jesus commanded something impossible and gave the power to do it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/ ; https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/studyguide_luk/luk_6.cfm
- **Precept Austin** applies it to salvation: the man admitted his helplessness, as a sinner must. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Gill** notes some differences in the manuscripts and versions. He insists the hand was made whole at once. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html

**v. 11 (filled with rage)**
- **Precept Austin:** the Greek word means a kind of senseless fury. Matthew and Mark say the leaders wanted to destroy Him. It quotes MacArthur on the contrast between God's truth and false religion in these two incidents. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Guzik:** their rage and plotting broke the Sabbath far worse than the healing did. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Gill:** they were enraged that they had no answer. He adds that they plotted later with the Herodians. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html

**v. 12 (a night of prayer)**
- **Guzik** sets this at a turning point of mounting opposition. He says Jesus, though God, sought the Father as a man would rather than relying on His own knowledge. He quotes Spurgeon on why Jesus went to the mountain. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin** quotes a writer praising Jesus' long night of prayer: we can't watch an hour, yet He watched whole nights for us. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 13 (twelve; "apostles")**
- **Guzik:** twelve to match the tribes of Israel, as the foundation of a new people. He explains "apostle" as "sent one" or ambassador. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin:** the number hinted that Jesus was Israel's messianic King. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 14 (Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew)**
- **Guzik** notes the pairs of brothers and fishermen. He identifies Bartholomew with Nathanael. He quotes Wiersbe: the list is in pairs because Jesus sent them out two by two. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the early church already knew these men well, so a bare list was enough. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/6.htm

**v. 16 (Judas son of James; Judas Iscariot)**
- **Guzik** identifies Judas son of James with Mark's Thaddaeus. He quotes Geldenhuys: Iscariot probably means "man from Kerioth," possibly the only Judean among the twelve. He adds that Jesus chose Judas knowing what he would do (John 6:70). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin** notes that Judas apparently also received authority over demons and disease. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 17 (the level place)**
- **Guzik** says some see "level place" as marking this off from Matthew's mountain. Others point out the local terrain could fit both descriptions. He thinks it is probably the same message as Matthew 5–7, but possibly given at a different time and place. He notes people came even from the Gentile cities of Tyre and Sidon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Poole** thinks it is a different discourse, because Matthew's and Luke's accounts differ so much. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/luke/6.htm

**v. 18 (healed of diseases and unclean spirits)**
- **Gill:** both bodily illness and demon possession were cured. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html

**v. 19 (power came from him)**
- **Guzik** links this to Mark 5:30: serving others cost Jesus something. He also observes that Jesus broke off the healing to teach. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Gill:** the people were convinced, and found by experience, that touching His body or clothes would heal them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html
- **Precept Austin:** miracles authenticated His claims but save no one. Only the Word lasts. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary

**v. 20 ("Blessed are you who are poor")** (the main point of disagreement)
- **Addressed to disciples.** Guzik says the sermon was placed between the choosing of the Twelve and their sending out, as training for them. Kelly and Preacher's Homiletical note that Luke speaks *to* the listeners ("you"), not *about* a class of people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-20.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-21.html
- **Mainly spiritual poverty:**
  - Guzik (Enduring Word, in your Pentecostal/charismatic group) says the Greek word means a beggar's poverty. Jesus mainly meant poverty of spirit, as Matthew words it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
  - Gill says both: poor in worldly things, having left all, and poor in spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html
  - Bible.org (Steven Cole's series) says Jesus is not blessing poverty itself but disciples who know they have nothing and rely on God. https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-25-how-live-happily-ever-after-luke-620-26
- **More literal or economic:**
  - Preacher's Homiletical sees every reason to think Luke means literal poverty. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-21.html
  - Coffman says the poor are blessed because they are less tempted to trust in riches. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-20.html
  - A Ligonier sermon (Reformed group) chooses to explore the economic reading. It focuses on disciples who gave up wealth for Christ, like Matthew. https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/beatitudes
- **Qualified by devotion to Jesus.** Desiring God (Baptist group) says the blessings are sweeping, but the context limits them. Not all poor people are blessed. The test is whether one's state is "on account of the Son of Man" (v. 22). https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/jesuss-warnings-to-the-comfortable
- **Matthew vs. Luke.** Ellicott thinks Jesus may have varied His wording on different occasions, rather than Luke dropping "in spirit." Another note on the same page says Luke means the same as Matthew and that Jesus was no flatterer of the poor as such. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/6-20.htm
- **"Is," not "will be."** Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) notes the present tense. BibleHub's topical article reads the kingdom as a present possession with full fulfilment later. It also notes Luke's wider theme of God turning things upside down (Luke 1:53; 4:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/ ; https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Blessed_are_the_poor_in_Luke_6_20.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** the kingdom in its full sense is enjoyed only hereafter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/6.htm
- **Clarke** (labelled Wesleyan/Methodist on StudyLight) simply refers readers to his notes on Matthew 5. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-20.html

**v. 21 (hunger and weep now)**
- **Gill:** literal hunger, but also spiritual hunger for righteousness, as in Matthew 5:6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html
- **Poole:** afflicted disciples are blessed, because God will wipe away their tears. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/luke/6.htm
- **Pulpit Homiletics:** no earthly joy fills the soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/luke/6.htm
- **Guzik:** Jesus didn't ignore physical need, but He aimed at sin's oppression. By giving hope in present hardship, He works against the spirit of violent revolution. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/

**v. 22 (hated "because of the Son of Man")**
- **Precept Austin:** these are true followers of Christ, rejected because the world rejected Him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Benson:** the One they suffer for is able and willing to repay them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/luke/6.htm

**v. 23 (rejoice; the prophets)**
- **Guzik:** the persecuted are in good company, the prophets'. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-6/
- **Precept Austin:** look past present suffering to the lasting reward. It cites how Israel mocked God's prophets (2 Chron 36). https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **Matthew Henry** likens it to the honour a soldier feels serving his prince. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/6-20.html
- **Pulpit Commentary** notes that the early church's leading teachers condemned believers who deliberately sought martyrdom because they took words like these too literally. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/6.htm

**v. 24 (woe to the rich)**
- **Gill:** not wealth itself. He means those who trust in riches, and above all those "rich" in their own righteousness, whose comfort is short-lived. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/luke-6.html
- **Benson:** woe if you seek your happiness in riches. Wealth's circumstances are especially dangerous to the soul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/benson/luke/6.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary** links it to the rich man and Lazarus. It says the parable's characters correct the idea that the rich are condemned just for being rich. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/6.htm
- **Precept Austin:** the four woes mirror the four blessings and fall on those who reject salvation. It quotes Steven Cole: the passage requires an eternal perspective. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-6-commentary
- **BibleHub's topical article:** Scripture does not condemn wealth as such (Joseph of Arimathea), only making an idol of it. https://biblehub.com/q/Meaning_of_Blessed_are_the_poor_in_Luke_6_20.htm
